- `feat:` or `feat(scope):` new feature

+1 on session-scoped SSE filtering — we're about to need this for our Jules integration.
We're adding Google Jules support (it's a session-based agent that uses polling), and we want the IDE experience to feel native. Our plan is to emit normalized jules.* Bus events — things like jules.run.created, status, plan, activity, artifact — and have the UI consume them through /event.
The problem is that /event currently broadcasts every bus event to every subscriber. For long-running agent sessions, that gets noisy fast. A simple /event?sessionID=... filter would help us:
- Reduce bandwidth and client-side processing (especially when activities and artifacts stream in frequently)
- Avoid the "SSE is super chatty" issues that have come up in performance discussions
- Make agent-run UIs more scalable as we add more providers down the road
On our end, we'll always include openCodeSessionID in the properties field of every jules.* event, so client-side routing works right away. Server-side filtering would just let us drop irrelevant events earlier in the pipeline.

### Use case: Write-time quality enforcement (linting on every edit)

Adding another concrete use case from the [aidevops](https://github.com/anomalyco/aidevops) framework.

We evaluated [Plankton](https://github.com/alexfazio/plankton) (write-time code quality enforcement via Claude Code hooks) and found the pattern compelling but not portable to OpenCode without native hook support.

**What Plankton does with hooks today:**

1. **PostToolUse on Edit/Write** — runs 20+ linters (shellcheck, ruff, biome, markdownlint, etc.) on every edited file, collects violations as structured JSON, and feeds them back to the agent immediately. The agent gets write-time feedback and produces better code during generation — not just through post-hoc correction at commit time.

2. **PreToolUse on Edit/Write** — blocks edits to linter config files (`.shellcheckrc`, `.ruff.toml`, `biome.json`, etc.). This prevents agents from "fixing" violations by weakening rules rather than fixing code. A real and common failure mode.

3. **PreToolUse on Bash** — enforces package manager policies (blocks `pip install`, suggests `uv`; blocks `npm`, suggests `bun`).

4. **Stop hook** — detects if any protected config files were modified during the session via `git diff`, prompts user to restore or keep.

**What we can do without hooks (current workaround):**

- Prompt-level instructions ("run shellcheck after editing shell files") — unreliable, especially with weaker models or long sessions
- Pre-commit git hooks — catches violations at commit time, not edit time (too late for the feedback loop benefit)
- MCP tools the agent can call explicitly — works but requires the agent to remember to call them

**What we'd do with native hooks:**

The same PostToolUse lint-on-edit pattern, but using our existing `linters-local.sh` infrastructure. We already have the linters, the structured output, and the fix automation — we just can't trigger them automatically on every tool call.

Watching PR #11525 with interest. The proposed `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` with exit code 2 = block + stderr feedback is exactly the protocol we'd use.

@bestouff Added a continuous monitoring mode! 🛡

```bash
# Re-download the updated script
curl -fsSL https://gist.githubusercontent.com/OmerFarukOruc/d1bf2bb1f6f4f01c3a0e63288ada7c94/raw/oc-cleanup -o ~/.local/bin/oc-cleanup
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/oc-cleanup

# Run guard mode — kills orphans exceeding 1GB RAM, checks every 60s
oc-cleanup guard

# Custom threshold (512MB) + check interval (30s)
oc-cleanup guard 512 30
```

It runs a continuous watchdog loop — checks for orphaned processes (no TTY), kills any that exceed the RAM threshold, and logs everything. Ctrl+C to stop with a summary of total kills.

You can also run it as a systemd user service for persistent background monitoring — see the [updated README](https://gist.github.com/OmerFarukOruc/d1bf2bb1f6f4f01c3a0e63288ada7c94) for the unit file.

Same issue here... Plus subscriber

```bash
stty -echo -icanon min 0 time 5
printf '\033]10;?\007\033]11;?\007\033]12;?\007\033]13;?\007\033]14;?\007\033]15;?\007\033]16;?\007\033]17;?\007\033]19;?\007'
dd bs=1 count=512 2>/dev/null | /bin/cat -v                                                                                                                                                                                                                     stty sane
```

The root issue is in the interaction between the `getPallette` function in opentui and ghostty. Here are the different responses to this command in ghostty and wezterm:

ghostty:
```
^[]10;rgb:cdcd/d6d6/f4f4^G^[]11;rgb:1e1e/1e1e/2e2e^G^[]12;rgb:f5f5/e0e0/dcdc^G%
```

wezterm:
```
^[]10;rgb:cdcd/d6d6/f4f4^[\^[]11;rgb:1e1e/1e1e/2e2e^[\^[]12;rgb:f5f5/e0e0/dcdc^[\^[]17;rgb:5858/5b5b/7070^[\^[]19;rgb:cdcd/d6d6/f4f4^[\% 
```

We see that ghostty gets back 10, 11, 12 (foreground, background, cursor), but does not return the 17/19. However neither of them return 13, 14, 15, 16, all of which are expected from special colors to return cleanly:

```js
class TerminalPallette implements TerminalPalletteDetector {
  ...
  private async querySpecialColors(timeoutMs = 1200): Promise<Record<number, Hex>> {
    const out = this.stdout
    const inp = this.stdin
    const results: Record<number, Hex> = {
      10: null,
      11: null,
      12: null,
      13: null,
      14: null,
      15: null,
      16: null,
      17: null,
      19: null,
    }
    ...
```

This should lead to both wezterm and ghostty hanging, but there is a backup idleTimer that times out after 150ms of inactivity (no escape sequences). Ghostty has a really chatty protocol, although I haven't looked too closely into why:
```
I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[I\x1B[
```

It sends a continuous stream of these escape sequences, preventing the inactivity timeout from triggering. 

The fix is in opetui, changing the timeout logic to only reset if the results table has been updated in the allotted time. It does not reset on unrelated escape sequences.

@TomLucidor

The fixes are provider/model-agnostic — they stabilize the request prefix so it is byte-for-byte identical across calls. Any provider with server-side prefix caching benefits automatically. See my reviewer's guide comment above for the full breakdown of each fix.

The specific model behind the provider does not matter — the changes are purely at the request layer. You can verify with any provider using `OPENCODE_CACHE_AUDIT=1` to see hit/miss per call.

**E2E failures** — pre-existing upstream issue, since fixed. CI is green now.

**Speculative decoding** — orthogonal. This PR only changes what is sent in the request, not how the server processes it.
